questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for main idea
questions.learningObjective: state the claim a short report hangs on
questions.stem: A local report reads 'Viele Städte haben ihre Innenstädte verändert. Bäume wurden gepflanzt und Parkplätze geschaffen. Einige Bewohner sagen, das Leben sei ruhiger geworden. Andere sagen, die Geschäfte hätten gelitten.' What is the main idea of that report?

options.text: The change has brought gains and complaints at once, and the report weighs both against each other
The change has solved the parking problem, and every resident quoted in it agrees on that
options.misconception: believes a report that names a benefit is endorsing it and ignoring disagreement

options.text: The residents oppose the changes, and the report explains why their opposition is justified
options.misconception: believes a report that quotes disagreement is arguing against the changes as a whole

options.text: The report recommends a second round of changes, and its evidence is the number of trees planted
options.misconception: believes a report that names a figure is recommending a further round of changes

questions.explanation: The main idea is the claim the whole passage hangs on, and here it is that one and the same change has produced good reports and bad ones at the same time. The two groups of residents are there to keep the claim open rather than to settle it, and a summary that reported only the trees or only the shops would drop half of what the passage says. The test is to ask which sentence a reader could delete without changing what the passage is about, and the answer is the two sentences naming what residents say, because both the gain and the complaint are instances of one position. A reader who looked for a recommendation has mistaken the genre, since a report describes and weighs while a proposal states what ought to happen next.
questions.hint: Ask which single sentence the other three are evidence for.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for main idea
questions.learningObjective: read a passage whose last sentence narrows the claim before it
questions.stem: A passage reads 'Ein Museum in einer kleinen Stadt hat seine Ausstellungsfläche verdoppelt. Im ersten Jahr stieg die Zahl der Besucher um ein Drittel. Die Stadtgemeinde spricht von einem Erfolg. Im zweiten Jahr jedoch ist der Zuwachs deutlich kleiner ausgefallen.' What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: A first-year success that the second year quietly puts in question, since the last sentence narrows it
A museum that has finished growing, since the two figures given show the rise has come to an end
options.misconception: believes two rising figures in a passage show that growth has come to an end

options.text: A town that misreads its own figures, since the passage treats a slowdown as a success
options.misconception: believes a passage that reports a slowdown is accusing somebody of misreading it

options.text: A museum whose funding must soon be cut, since a smaller rise makes the running costs too high
options.misconception: believes a slower rise in visitors is evidence that the funding must be withdrawn

questions.explanation: The passage is built as a report that keeps one figure in the open and then closes with a fact that narrows it, and the main idea is the narrowing rather than either figure on its own. The last sentence does the work, because it says the second year was smaller, and a reader who stops at the third sentence will have missed the qualification altogether. A main idea is not the number that stands out and it is not the writer's verdict either, since the passage reports the town's verdict in the third sentence rather than endorsing it. The useful habit is to read the last sentence of such a passage first and then ask which of the earlier sentences it qualifies, because the qualifying word, here jedoch, is where the real claim usually sits.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence the writer has used to limit what the earlier sentences claim.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for detail
questions.learningObjective: find the phrase in a passage that answers a given question
questions.stem: A notice says 'Der Verein vereinbart die Mitgliedsbeiträge jährlich im März. Kinder zahlen die Hälfte.' Which detail answers the question 'Wer zahlt im März weniger?'

options.text: Kinder, because the passage names them as the group paying half of the usual amount
Erwachsene, because the passage names the standard rate for members over eighteen years of age
options.misconception: believes a passage naming children as reduced payers must be naming adults as the ones paying less

options.text: Der Verein, because the passage says the amounts are arranged by the association every March
options.misconception: believes the body that sets an amount is the group that pays the reduced amount

options.text: Neue Mitglieder, because the passage says anyone who joins after March pays nothing that year
options.misconception: believes a mention of the month of payment implies that newcomers pay nothing at all

questions.explanation: A detail question is answered by a phrase the passage actually contains, and here that phrase is the clause saying children pay half, which names the group and the amount in one stretch. The trap is to answer with something the passage mentions without it being the answer, which is what the association and the month of March both are: they belong to the setting rather than to the reply. A second trap is reading past the comparison, since the passage never says what adults pay, and a reader who assumes the adult rate is being contrasted has added a fact the text does not contain. The habit worth building is to find the sentence that carries the question's own words before reading anything else, because a short passage usually has exactly one and the rest is context.
questions.hint: Underline the words the question itself uses and look for them in the passage.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for detail
questions.learningObjective: separate a daily figure in a passage from a span of dates
questions.stem: A notice reads 'Die Stadtwerke erneuern in diesem Jahr die Wasserleitungen im Viertel Nord. Die Arbeiten beginnen am 6. April und sollen bis Ende Juli dauern. Währenddessen ist die Versorgung in den Häusern täglich zwischen 8 und 12 Uhr unterbrochen.' Which detail answers 'Wann ist die Versorgung unterbrochen?'

options.text: Zwischen 8 und 12 Uhr, because that is the daily window the passage gives for the interruption
Vom 6. April bis Ende Juli, because the passage gives those dates as the daily interruption window
options.misconception: believes the dates of the work are the same thing as the daily window of interruption

options.text: Nur im Viertel Nord, because the passage limits the interruption to that single district
options.misconception: believes naming a district in a passage answers a question about the hour of a day

options.text: Während der ganzen Arbeiten, because the passage says the supply stops for the whole of the work
options.misconception: believes the passage states a daily window that is really a span of several months

questions.explanation: The question asks when the interruption happens on an ordinary day, and the only phrase that answers it is the window between 8 and 12 Uhr, which the passage attaches to the word täglich. The dates in the passage are the span of the whole building work and answer a different question, namely how long the project will take, and the district answers a where-question rather than a when-question. The word täglich is the hinge, because it tells a reader that the hours repeat every day and that the dates are therefore the outer limit rather than the daily figure. A habit worth building is to underline the phrase that repeats the question's own words, since a notice usually contains exactly one such phrase and everything else is either setting or warning.
questions.hint: Ask whether the question is about one day, about the whole project or about a place.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for tone
questions.learningObjective: name the tone of a short comment from the words it chooses
questions.stem: A short comment reads 'Es ist höchste Zeit, dass hier einmal etwas passiert. Seit Jahren wird zugesehen, wie die Halle immer leerer wird, und alle haben sich daran gewöhnt, wegzusehen.' What tone does the writer take?

options.text: Reproachful and urgent, since the opening calls for action and the closing assigns blame to everyone
Neutral and descriptive, since the passage only reports what has happened in the hall over the years
options.misconception: believes a passage that names a problem must be neutral about that problem

options.text: Cheerful, since gewöhnt shows that the readers have accepted the situation and can live with it
options.misconception: believes a word such as gewöhnt always signals contentment rather than resignation

options.text: Regretful about a lost building, since the passage says the hall has become emptier than it was
options.misconception: believes a passage describing an emptying hall must be mourning the loss of a building

questions.explanation: Tone is carried by the choice of words rather than by the information, and this passage marks it in two places: höchste Zeit announces that the writer has run out of patience, and wegzusehen names a deliberate failure to act which the writer attributes to everyone, the readers included. The same facts could be reported in a neutral register, and that is the test of whether a tone judgement is grounded, because if the facts alone fixed the tone there would be nothing left to argue about. Wegsehen is a content word that a neutral version would have replaced with something tun, and the replacement would leave the sentence grammatical while removing the blame. A reader who takes gewöhnt as contentment has read one word in isolation instead of reading the construction around it.
questions.hint: Ask which two words in the passage could not appear in a neutral report.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading for tone
questions.learningObjective: put sentences of a comment in an order that builds the tone
questions.stem: Four sentences have been cut out of a comment and are in the wrong order. Which sequence restores a passage whose tone builds from observation to reproach?

options.text: und alle haben sich daran gewöhnt, wegzusehen.
Seit Jahren wird zugesehen, wie die Halle immer leerer wird,
Es ist höchste Zeit, dass hier einmal etwas passiert.
Man gewöhnt sich schnell daran, wenn nichts geschieht.

questions.explanation: The passage has to open on something the writer can see, since a reproach needs a fact behind it, so the sentence about the emptying hall gives the reader the situation before any judgement is passed on it. The second step is the complaint itself, and only once höchste Zeit has named the demand can wegzusehen close the first sentence as a charge against everybody, the reader included. The final sentence generalises the excuse the writer is attacking, and that is what gives the comment its edge, because it says the waiting has become a habit rather than a single failure. Put the demand first and the reader has nothing to attach it to, which is why the order matters even though every sentence is grammatical on its own.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence has to come before a judgement can be made at all.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A writer's attitude and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: read an attitude out of the frame rather than out of any adjective
questions.stem: A piece reads 'Das neue Durchfahrtsverbot ist eine gute Idee, sagt die Firma. Die Anwohner verlieren ihre Parkplätze, und der Verkehr wird sich in die Nebenstraßen verlagern. Nichts davon hat die Firma erwähnt.' What is the writer's attitude to the firm, and what supports it?

options.text: Sceptical, because the writer quotes the firm's praise and then lists two consequences the firm passed over
Supportive, because the writer reports the firm's judgement accurately before turning to the details
options.misconception: believes a passage that quotes praise is endorsing the speaker who offered it

options.text: Indifferent, because the passage sets out both sides of the question without taking a position
options.misconception: believes a passage that lists consequences without comment is refusing to take a side

options.text: Rebuking, because the writer states outright that the firm's announcement was made in bad faith
options.misconception: believes a remark about what a speaker omitted is the same as accusing that speaker of bad faith

questions.explanation: The attitude is carried by the frame rather than by any adjective, and the frame here is a report of what the firm said, followed by two consequences, followed by a remark about what was not said. A writer who agreed with the firm would either have dropped the two consequences or explained why they did not matter, and a writer who was neutral would have stopped before the last sentence, since noting an omission is itself a judgement. The evidence is the omission made explicit, which is stronger than any editorial comment because it lets a reader check the gap against the announcement. A reader who takes the quoted praise for the writer's own view has missed that it sits inside a clause with sagt, and a reader who calls this a rebuke is claiming more than the passage claims.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking inside each sentence, and whether the writer ever agrees.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A writer's attitude and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: explain how an unmarked passage reveals an attitude and what to cite
questions.stem: A learner has to say what attitude a passage takes towards a proposal, and the passage contains no evaluative adjective at all. Explain how the writer signals it anyway, and say what a reader should quote when justifying the answer.

answer.exemplar: The attitude comes from the frame and from what has been selected, not from an adjective: a verb of saying attributes praise to somebody other than the writer, a pair of consequences is then listed, and a closing sentence remarks on what that speaker left out. The expected answer therefore cites those three features, and a reader should quote the naming of the speaker and the sentence about the omission, because together they show whom the writer is standing with. A version that only says the tone is critical is an assertion and not a reading.

questions.explanation: A passage can take a position without ever using a word like gut or schlecht, and the position is then carried by three things a learner can point at. The first is attribution, since praise inside a clause with sagt belongs to the firm and not to the writer. The second is selection, because a writer who agreed would not have chosen those two consequences or, at the very least, would have answered them somewhere. The third is the remark about the omission, which no neutral description would make at all. The answer a reader should justify is built from those three, and a version that only says the tone is critical is an assertion rather than a reading. Citing the naming of the speaker and the closing remark is what turns a judgement into something a marker can check.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer has attributed, selected and pointed out.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A text's purpose and how it is signalled
questions.learningObjective: say what a reader is expected to do with a text and how the text shows it
questions.stem: A notice reads 'Am Montag, 14. April, um 9 Uhr, findet im Saal 2 die öffentliche Anhörung zur Änderung der Parkgebühren statt. Nähere Informationen erhalten Sie im Sekretariat.' What is the purpose of the notice, and what marks it?

options.text: To inform readers of an event and of where to ask more, which the date, the room and the office show
To persuade readers to attend, which the neutral wording and the named office both show
options.misconception: believes a neutral set of facts in a notice is an attempt to persuade its readers

options.text: To report a decision already taken, which the present form of findet is there to show
options.misconception: believes a present-tense verb in a notice reports a decision that has been taken

options.text: To advertise a service, which the mention of the park fees and of the secretariat is there to show
options.misconception: believes any mention of a fee and an office makes a text an advertisement for a service

questions.explanation: Purpose is settled by what a reader is expected to do, and here the reader is expected to know when and where something happens and where to ask questions, which is information rather than persuasion or reporting. The signals are structural rather than emotional: a date, an hour, a named room and a named office are what an information notice is built from, while a persuasive notice would have to argue for coming rather than simply record the arrangements. The present of findet does not report a decision taken, because the event is still ahead of the readers, and a fee being mentioned does not make a text an advertisement, since the fee is the subject of the hearing and not something on offer. A learner who expects emotional wording will find none and should not conclude the text has no purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is meant to do after finishing the text.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An author's argument in an original passage
questions.learningObjective: name the claim and the evidence in a short original argument
questions.stem: A short article reads 'Viele Schulen haben ihre Büchereien geschlossen. Wer Schulbücher kaufen will, muss inzwischen in den nächsten Ort fahren. Ein Verleiger liefert deshalb zu fast allen Titeln nur noch digital aus. Das trifft vor allem Familien ohne Auto und mit kleinen Kindern. Die Initiative fordert deshalb, die Büchereien wieder zu öffnen.' What is the argument the passage is making?

options.text: That closing the libraries has left one group of families hardest hit, and that they should be reopened
That school libraries are no longer needed, because almost every title is now available as a download
options.misconception: believes a demand at the end of a passage is only a description of what already exists

options.text: That the publishers are at fault, and that schools should ask them for paper copies again
options.misconception: believes naming a publisher as a cause makes that publisher the target of the demand

options.text: That most schoolchildren now read on screens, and that the article reports this as proven
options.misconception: believes a passage that mentions digital delivery has proved that children read on screens

questions.explanation: An argument has a claim, evidence and the link between them, and the claim here is the demand in the last sentence, which says the libraries should be reopened. The evidence is the two facts before it, namely the journey to the next town and the digital-only supply, and the link is the sentence saying which group those two facts hit hardest, because that is what turns a description of a closure into a case for undoing it. A passage that only reported the facts would stop after the second sentence and ask for nothing. A reader who thinks the article puts the blame on the publishers has read a cause as a target, since the demand is addressed to the schools, and a reader who thinks it proves anything about children has picked up a fact the passage never states.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence would be missing if the passage only reported what happened.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A claim the evidence does not support
questions.learningObjective: judge whether the evidence in a sentence carries the claim attached to it
questions.stem: A writer says 'In diesem Jahr haben 400 Besucher die Ausstellung besucht. Die Ausstellung ist deshalb ein Erfolg.' Which judgement on that passage is right?

options.text: The evidence is a single number, and it does not carry a general claim about the exhibition as a whole
The evidence is a number, and a number is exactly the kind of support a claim about success needs
options.misconception: believes a bare figure is by itself enough to carry a general claim about an outcome

options.text: The evidence is a number, and the claim is therefore weaker than the number makes it appear
options.misconception: believes a single figure cannot support a general claim even when the claim is modest

options.text: The evidence is a number, and a text that carries a number is likely to be in a written register
options.misconception: believes the presence of a figure in a text is a sign of the register it is written in

questions.explanation: A claim is supported when the evidence is of the right kind and covers the same ground, and a single count of visitors does neither for a general word like Erfolg, which covers quality, reach and lasting effect. The connective deshalb makes the gap visible, because it announces that a figure and a judgement are being tied together, and that is exactly where a reader should look. What the figure does support is a narrower claim, such as the exhibition was well visited this year, and a careful version of the sentence would say that instead. A learner who defends the passage by pointing out that there is a number has read support as mere presence, and a register judgement taken from the presence of a figure is a separate error, since figures turn up in notices and reports as well.
questions.hint: Ask what range of fact the word in the claim covers, and what range the number covers.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A claim the evidence does not support
questions.learningObjective: screen sentences for claims their own evidence can carry
questions.stem: Three sentences from a student essay are set out for inspection. Which three are claims that the evidence given inside the same sentence actually supports?

options.text: Der Bericht nennt drei Messwerte und dazu die Messmethode, also kann ein Leser die Werte nachvollziehen.
Der Bericht nennt drei Messwerte, also ist damit die ganze Lage an dieser Schule beschrieben.
options.misconception: believes three measurements of one thing describe a situation in general

options.text: Die Autorin nennt fünf Quellen, also hat sie alle fünf auch ausführlich ausgewertet.
options.misconception: believes naming a source in a text is the same as having worked through it

options.text: Die Autorin nennt fünf Quellen, also kann ein Leser die Herkunft der Angaben prüfen.
Der Verfasser nennt Titel und Jahr des Werks, also lässt sich die Angabe nachschlagen.

questions.explanation: Three of the five claims are the kind a sentence's own evidence can carry. Naming the measurement method beside three figures lets a reader follow the figures up, naming five sources lets a reader find where the claims came from, and giving a title and a year lets a reader look the reference up. The two rejected claims each step further than the sentence goes. A source named in a text may have been opened and never used, and three measurements of one aspect of one school say nothing about the situation in general. The habit behind all of this is to ask what a reader could do with the evidence given, because a claim that makes nothing checkable is a claim the sentence has not earned, however confident its connective sounds.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could actually do with the evidence each sentence supplies.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An inference that follows and one that does not
questions.learningObjective: build an inference out of the text and reject the ones that add to it
questions.stem: A passage says 'Die Bahn hat die Verbindung nach Warnemünde abgeschafft. Seitdem ist die Zahl der Pendler in der Stadt gesunken.' Which inference does the passage license?

options.text: Fewer people now travel to work by train, because the line they used has closed
Fewer people now work in the city, because the number of commuters has fallen
options.misconception: believes a fall in the number of commuters proves there are fewer jobs in the city

options.text: The railway plans to restore the line, because the number of commuters has fallen
options.misconception: believes a fall in commuters is evidence that the railway intends to bring the line back

options.text: The city has lost its station, because the railway has withdrawn the service
options.misconception: believes withdrawing a service means the station building itself has been taken away

questions.explanation: An inference has to be built out of what the passage says and nothing more, and the chain here is short: the line has closed, the number of commuters has fallen, so the number travelling to work by that train must have fallen with it. The other three options each add something the passage never mentions, whether that is a change in the number of jobs, a plan at the railway, or the fate of a building. A learner who finds an inference attractive because it sounds reasonable is applying outside knowledge instead of the text, and a good check is to ask whether the second sentence could be true even if the first were not, which for the first option it could not and for the other three it easily could.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second sentence could be true if the first sentence were false.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An inference that follows and one that does not
questions.learningObjective: choose the one inference a passage will bear
questions.stem: A passage reads 'Die Stadt hat den alten Bahnsteig nicht abgerissen, sondern für einen Flohmarkt freigegeben. An drei Samstagen im September kamen jeweils rund 400 Besucher. Die Stadt überlegt nun, den Platz im Winter ebenfalls zu öffnen.' What can be inferred from it?

options.text: The city has found the site worth keeping, since three Saturdays each drew about four hundred visitors
The city is short of money, since a site given over to a market cannot be used for anything else
options.misconception: believes a decision to use a site for a market is evidence that no money is available

options.text: The railway wants the platform back, since a flea market is only ever a temporary solution
options.misconception: believes a change of use by a city implies the former owner wants the site returned

options.text: The winter here is mild, since the city is willing to open the site in the colder months
options.misconception: believes a plan to open a site in winter is evidence about the climate of a region

questions.explanation: The inference that holds is the modest one, because three Saturdays with about four hundred visitors each is a result, and a city that has just begun considering a winter opening has found the summer worth repeating. The other three options each require a fact the passage does not supply: nothing in it mentions money, the railway is not said to have any view at all, and a plan for the winter says nothing about the weather. That last one is the commonest trap in reading, because opening a site in winter feels as though it must imply something about the climate, whereas the passage records only an intention. The test that catches all three is to ask whether a reader could keep every sentence true and still reject the inference, and here they could.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three rejected inferences needs a fact the passage never gives.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An author's bias marked by a word choice
questions.learningObjective: find the words that carry a verdict in an otherwise flat report
questions.stem: A report writes 'Die Liste der funktionierenden Kitas ist lang, während einige Einrichtungen den Anforderungen nicht genügen.' What does the wording do?

options.text: It loads one side with a positive term and the other with a negative one, so the verdict arrives inside the nouns
It reports both sides in neutral terms, so the reader is left to weigh the evidence without steering
options.misconception: believes naming two sides of a question makes a sentence neutral whatever the words are

options.text: It uses two passive constructions, so the sentence hides who is responsible for the failing facilities
options.misconception: believes a sentence is biased because it uses the passive rather than because of the words chosen

options.text: It contrasts a long list with a few facilities, so the sentence warns the reader about a small number
options.misconception: believes the word some in a report is a warning and not a softener of the numbers given

questions.explanation: Bias in a factual report usually arrives through the words chosen for the two sides, and here the two nouns do the work: a facility that meets the standard is functioning, and one that does not fails to meet requirements, so the sentence never has to say which side it is on. The softener einige does a quieter job of the same kind, since it makes the second group sound like a handful while the first is a long list, and that asymmetry is a numerical claim smuggled in with a quantifier. A reader who wants to check the balance can ask what the sentence would look like with the two nouns exchanged, and it would not be neutral, because the positive term is the flattering one. A judgement about bias made from the grammar alone will always miss this, and so will one made from the presence of a passive.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two nouns would flatter the group it describes.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: An author's bias marked by a word choice
questions.learningObjective: read a bias that enters through an adjective about the other side
questions.stem: A report reads 'Nur wenige Beschäftigte nutzen die neuen Arbeitsplätze, und das Team vermisst die ruhige Atmosphäre des alten Raums fast einhellig.' What does the wording do?

options.text: It praises the old arrangement and says nothing kind about the new, so the verdict sits in the adjectives
It reports a small number and a shared opinion, so both facts are given without any steering
options.misconception: believes a report that states two facts has made no judgement about either one

options.text: It claims the new workplaces are unused, and the opinion is given as the reason for keeping them
options.misconception: believes an opinion quoted in a passage is the writer's own reason for keeping the old rooms

options.text: It repeats what the employees said, and the repetition is what makes the passage sound balanced
options.misconception: believes repeating a group's opinion in a sentence shows that the writer is neutral

questions.explanation: The sentence reports a number and an opinion, and the opinion is where the bias sits, because the old room is given a quality worth missing while the new workplaces are given nothing at all. The second clause is where a reader should stop, since fast einhellig presents a shared preference as a settled fact about the staff and so removes any need to report anybody who disagreed. That is the ordinary way bias enters an otherwise flat report, and it is worth checking by substitution, because the sentence would be just as grammatical if it said the staff had welcomed the change. A reader who counts the facts and finds two correct ones has not asked what the adjectives are doing to the weight those facts carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the sentence would say if the writer's opinion were the opposite one.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A euphemism and what it conceals
questions.learningObjective: read a neutral phrase as a report of an unwelcome fact
questions.stem: A notice says 'Die Abteilung wurde neu ausgerichtet' on a page where a list of names would otherwise have appeared. What does the notice conceal?

options.text: The dismissals, because it reports a change in staffing without ever saying that staff have gone
The promotions, because it reports a change in staffing that in fact involved senior staff leaving
options.misconception: believes a euphemism about staffing conceals a promotion rather than a departure

options.text: The pay rise, because it reports a change in pay that would have appeared in the same place

The closing formula then opens the signature block, and the name of the person who signs comes last, with i. V. marking that the person is signing on behalf of a named office rather than personally. The rejected piece uses the English order of month and day, which in German would be written 14.04.2026, and it is the only one of the five a reader would actually get wrong rather than merely find unusual.
questions.hint: Ask which piece has to come first, and write the date the German way.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A time expression and whether it needs a preposition
questions.learningObjective: say which preposition a day, a month and a date take in German
questions.stem: A speaker says 'Ich fahre am Montag nach Hamburg und bin am Freitag zurück.' Which part of that sentence needs a preposition?

options.text: Both time expressions, because am introduces a day of the week and a date alike
Neither, because the name of a day of the week never takes a preposition in German
options.misconception: believes a day of the week never takes a preposition in a time expression

options.text: Only the first, because a day of the week needs one while a date does not
options.misconception: believes a day of the week and a calendar date are governed by different prepositions

options.text: Both, but the second may be left out in speech because the context makes it clear
options.misconception: believes a date can lose its preposition in speech while a day of the week cannot

questions.explanation: A day of the week, a month and a date all come with a preposition, and in this sentence the preposition is am in both places, since am introduces a weekday and a date alike. The preposition is what turns a bare name into a time, so Freitag on its own is a noun and not an adverbial, and a reader who hears it without am will take the day as the subject. A weekday appears without a preposition only when the word names a repetition, as in montags, and that is a different word from Montag. Nothing in the pair can simply be dropped in speech, because the preposition is carrying the work, and the test is to ask what the phrase would be without it.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase would be if the preposition were removed.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A time expression and whether it needs a preposition
questions.learningObjective: screen sentences for the preposition the German time rules require
questions.stem: A grammar drill lists five sentences and says that three of them give their time expression the way German rules require. Which three are those?

options.text: Wir treffen uns am 5. Mai 2026 im Konferenzraum.
Wir treffen uns 5. Mai 2026 im Konferenzraum.
options.misconception: leaves a date without am, and a bare date names a day rather than a time

options.text: Der Kurs beginnt im Mai 2026 im neuen Gebäude.
Wir treffen uns am Dienstag im Konferenzraum.
Der Kurs beginnt im 2026 im neuen Gebäude.
options.misconception: puts im in front of a year, where German uses in instead of it

questions.explanation: Three of the five write the time the way German requires. A day of the week, a date and a month are each introduced by a preposition, and the preposition changes with the size of the unit: am for a weekday and for a date, im for a month and for a season. The two rejected sentences go wrong in opposite ways. The first drops the preposition from a date, which leaves a noun naming a day rather than a time, and a reader hearing it will take the day as the subject of the sentence. The other puts a month in front of a year, where the two units are of different size and the preposition has to match the larger one, so a year takes in. The pattern is short and worth learning as a table of three prepositions and their units.
questions.hint: Ask how large the unit of time is, and which preposition matches that size.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A measure word construction
questions.learningObjective: name the case of a unit in a phrase introduced by von
questions.stem: A text says 'Das Gebäude ist 30 Meter hoch und hat eine Breite von zwanzig Metern.' What has the second phrase done differently from the first?

options.text: It names the measure in a genitive, with the unit in the genitive after von
It names the measure in a nominative, with the unit in the nominative after von
options.misconception: believes the unit in a phrase with von is in the nominative rather than the genitive

options.text: It names the measure in a dative, with the unit in the dative after von
options.misconception: believes a phrase with von puts its noun in the dative rather than the genitive

options.text: It names the measure in an accusative, with the unit in the accusative after von
options.misconception: believes a phrase with von puts its noun in the accusative rather than the genitive

questions.explanation: A phrase introduced by von that names a measure takes the genitive, so von zwanzig Metern is a genitive of measure and the metre is the unit of the width rather than the object of a verb. The first sentence does it differently by making the number and the unit the predicate directly, which is the ordinary form when the figure comes first. A learner who expects von to introduce an accusative object, as it does in von dem Kollegen, will write von zwanzig Meter and produce a phrase that is not German at all. The same genitive of measure appears in eine Länge von drei Metern and ein Gewicht von zwei Kilo, and the unit changes form with the case, so a plural unit takes an -n.
questions.hint: Ask what von does to a noun phrase that names a measurement.

questions.topic: A measure word construction
questions.learningObjective: read two constructions of measurement in one short passage
questions.stem: A passage reads 'Die Brücke ist 180 Meter lang. Sie hat eine Spannweite von 90 Metern und eine Höhe von zwölf Metern über der Fahrbahn.' What does the passage show about measurement?

options.text: The first sentence makes the unit a predicate, and the other two use a genitive of measure after von
The first sentence uses a genitive of measure, and the other two make the unit a predicate
options.misconception: believes the sentence with the unit straight after the number is the genitive one

options.text: All three sentences use a genitive of measure, and only the numbers are different between them
options.misconception: believes every sentence naming a length in a bridge description uses a genitive

options.text: The first two use a genitive of measure, and the third makes the unit a predicate
options.misconception: believes the genitive of measure appears only where the unit follows the figure

questions.explanation: The passage shows both constructions side by side, and the difference is where the figure stands. In the first sentence the measurement is the predicate of the bridge, which is the ordinary form when the number comes first, while in the other two the measurement is a noun phrase in the genitive introduced by von, so von 90 Metern and von zwölf Metern name an attribute of the bridge rather than its predicate. A learner who reads all three as the same construction has not noticed that von changes both the case and the form of the unit, since a plural unit takes an -n in the genitive and that is visible in both of the Metern. The pattern to hold is short: figure and unit as a predicate, or von plus a genitive, never von plus an uninflected unit.

questions.topic: A compound noun that changes the meaning
questions.learningObjective: show how a compound names a different thing rather than a longer name
questions.stem: A writer uses 'Der Schlüssel liegt auf dem Tisch' and later 'Das Schlüsselkind wohnt bei uns.' What has the compound done to the meaning?

options.text: It has named a different thing, because a compound is not a longer name but another noun entirely
It has named the same thing more precisely, because a compound always adds detail to the first noun
options.misconception: believes adding a word in front of a noun only ever makes a phrase more precise

options.text: It has kept the meaning and changed only the gender, because a compound always changes the gender
options.misconception: believes a compound noun is a set of readings of one noun rather than a different noun

options.text: It has kept the meaning and changed only the article, because the article is what a compound alters
options.misconception: believes the only thing a compound changes about a noun is the article that goes with it

questions.explanation: A German compound is not a longer name for one thing but a different thing altogether, and the article is the quickest evidence, because it changes from der in Der Schlüssel to das in Das Schlüsselkind. What the second word contributes is not detail but a new kind of thing, a child rather than an object of metal, and the same is true of das Schlüsselbrett and der Schlüsseldienst, which name a board and a service. A learner who treats a compound as a habit of writing things in one word will expect the two to be related in meaning, and a learner who thinks the gender causes the change has the evidence backwards, since the change in referent is what the gender is recording. The rule to hold on to is short: a noun in front makes a new noun.
questions.hint: Ask which article goes with the compound, and compare it with the simple noun.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A compound noun that changes the meaning
questions.learningObjective: say what happens to a preposition that goes inside a compound
questions.stem: A text says 'Nach der Besprechung kam die Entscheidung' and then writes 'Die Nachbesprechung war kurz.' What has the compound done with the preposition?

options.text: It has read the preposition as a plain stem, so the compound names a following discussion and not a moment
It has kept the preposition's usual sense, so the compound can only ever be read as a point in time
options.misconception: believes a preposition inside a compound can only ever be read as a fixed point in time

options.text: It has taken the first word from the end of the phrase the compound was built from
options.misconception: believes a compound takes its first word from the end of the phrase it came from

options.text: It has dropped the preposition entirely, because careful German forbids one inside a compound
options.misconception: believes careful German forbids a preposition inside a compound noun altogether

questions.explanation: A German compound can be built out of any word at all, and a preposition inside it keeps none of its old work, so a preposition plus noun in a compound is read as one plain stem. The Nach- in Nachbesprechung therefore has nothing to do with a point in time, which is what nach means in the phrase it came from, and the compound names the discussion that follows another discussion rather than any moment in particular. A learner who hears a preposition in a compound and expects the usual sense will misread the whole word. The sign is the ending, since a compound takes the gender and number of its final element and then a normal adjective ending, and that is also why a writer can coin a new compound in the course of a text whenever one is needed.
questions.hint: Ask what work the preposition is doing now that it is inside a compound.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A translation that preserves register
questions.learningObjective: choose the German version that keeps the register of a formal sentence
questions.stem: A letter in English reads 'Please find enclosed my report, which I trust will meet with your approval.' Which German version keeps the register of the original?

options.text: In der Anlage finden Sie meinen Bericht, von dem ich hoffe, dass er Ihre Zustimmung findet.
In der Anlage ist mein Bericht, der bestimmt toll bei dir ankommt.
options.misconception: drops to a familiar address form and adds a modal particle the original has not got

options.text: Hier ist der Bericht, und ich hoffe sehr, dass er Ihnen super gefällt und passt.
options.misconception: replaces the formal noun of the enclosure with a plain word and adds a modal particle

options.text: Anbei mein Bericht, ich hoffe der kommt bei Ihnen gut an und passt dann auch.
options.misconception: builds a spoken sentence with a missing subject and a modal the original has not got

questions.explanation: The English sentence is a formal business formula, and the German version has to keep three things at once: the polite address, the formal vocabulary of the enclosure, and a construction that lets the hope be expressed about something other than the speaker. The first does all three, since Sie marks distance, Anlage is the term the business register uses rather than Anbei, and a relative clause introduced by von carries the hope without making the writer its subject. The second and third collapse into a familiar register the moment the address or a modal particle appears, and the fourth does something subtler, since it uses a modal in a relative clause and leaves the subordinate clause without a subject, which reads as speech on paper. A translation of this kind is judged on register, and sense alone is what all four share.
questions.hint: Ask which three things about the original would be lost in the shorter versions.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: A translation that preserves register
questions.learningObjective: translate a formal English request and name what carries the register
questions.stem: Stage one: translate 'I should be grateful if you could confirm receipt by Friday' into a German sentence of a formal business register. Stage two: name the three things in your version that carry the register, and say which of them a learner is most likely to drop.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: 'Ich wäre Ihnen dankbar, wenn Sie den Eingang bis Freitag bestätigen könnten.' Stage two: the three carriers are the address form Sie, the verb of obligation and the polite conditional with könnten, and the one most often lost is the address form, because a learner who has practised du socially reaches for it without noticing and the result is grammatical German in the wrong register.

questions.explanation: The two stages are worth pairing because the second is what makes the first a translation rather than a paraphrase. The English sentence is a formal request, and a German version has to be formal in the same three places: the address form, the verb that carries the obligation, and the conditional that softens it. A condition with könnte is the standard way of saying what English does with a modal plus a conditional, and dropping it for a bare imperative gives a correct German sentence in a completely different register. The address form is the easiest thing to lose, since a learner who has practised du socially will reach for it without noticing, and the result is a request that would embarrass the sender rather than the reader. A closing formula carries as much register as the sentence itself and belongs in the same judgement.
questions.hint: Ask which features of the original would be missing from a plain imperative.
